stem: Which statements about transmission at the neuromuscular junction are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The motor neuron action potential opens voltage gated Ca2+ channels in the axon terminal, and Ca2+ entry triggers acetylcholine release.
Acetylcholine opens nicotinic receptor channels that pass both Na+ and K+, and the net inward current depolarizes the end plate.
The end plate potential is an all or none action potential.
The end plate potential is normally several times larger than needed to reach threshold, so each neuronal action potential produces one muscle action potential.
Acetylcholine is taken back into the nerve terminal intact, which is how the signal ends.
The muscle action potential is generated by voltage gated Na+ channels in the sarcolemma next to the end plate.
why: The nerve action potential opens Ca2+ channels, Ca2+ triggers exocytosis of acetylcholine, and acetylcholine opens a nonselective cation channel on the end plate. The resulting end plate potential is graded, but it is so large (the safety factor) that it always brings the neighboring sarcolemma to threshold and fires a muscle action potential through voltage gated Na+ channels. Acetylcholinesterase then breaks the transmitter down in the cleft.
whyNot: Belongs. Ca2+ entry into the terminal is the trigger for vesicle fusion; block those channels and no transmitter is released.
Belongs. The nicotinic receptor is a ligand gated channel permeable to both cations, and more Na+ enters than K+ leaves, so the membrane depolarizes.
Wrong. The end plate potential is graded with the amount of acetylcholine. It triggers the action potential; it is not one.
Belongs. This large safety factor is why transmission at a healthy junction never fails, and why losing receptors in myasthenia gravis matters so much.
Wrong. Acetylcholine is hydrolyzed by acetylcholinesterase in the cleft, and only the choline is taken back up. This option describes reuptake of transmitters such as norepinephrine.
Belongs. The end plate itself has few voltage gated Na+ channels; the end plate current spreads to the surrounding membrane, which fires the action potential.

stem: A single twitch is recorded from an isolated skeletal muscle fiber. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The latent period runs from the stimulus to the first rise in tension and includes the action potential, Ca2+ release, and the first crossbridge attachments.
Tension rises during the contraction phase as more crossbridges attach and the elastic elements in series are stretched.
The relaxation phase reflects Ca2+ being pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, so crossbridges stop cycling and tension falls.
The muscle action potential lasts about as long as the twitch.
A stronger single stimulus to this one fiber produces a taller twitch.
why: A twitch has three parts, and each is limited by a different process. The latent period is set by the electrical and chemical steps before force appears. The contraction phase is set by how fast crossbridges attach and how much elastic slack must be taken up. The relaxation phase is set by how fast SERCA removes Ca2+. The action potential itself is over within a couple of milliseconds, long before force peaks.
whyNot: Belongs. Nothing mechanical shows up until the action potential has spread down the T tubules, Ca2+ has been released, and heads have begun to bind.
Belongs. Force at the tendon rises only as heads attach and pull the tendon and other elastic structures taut.
Belongs. Relaxation is an active, ATP using process, because SERCA has to pump Ca2+ away before troponin lets go.

Wrong. The action potential lasts 1 to 2 ms; the twitch lasts tens of milliseconds. This difference is exactly what allows summation, because a second action potential can arrive while the first twitch is still going.

Wrong. One fiber is all or none. It fires or it does not, and a suprathreshold stimulus of any size gives the same twitch. Force grading by stimulus strength happens in a whole muscle, where a bigger shock recruits more fibers.

stem: Which statements about isometric and isotonic contractions are correct? Select all that apply.
options: In an isometric contraction crossbridges cycle and tension develops, but the muscle does not shorten because the load is not moved.
In a concentric contraction the muscle shortens while it develops tension.
An eccentric contraction occurs when the load exceeds the tension the muscle produces, so the muscle lengthens while it is active.
Shortening velocity increases as the load increases.
An isotonic contraction begins with an isometric phase that lasts until tension matches the load.
A muscle lowering a heavy weight slowly is contracting concentrically.
why: Whether a muscle shortens, holds, or lengthens depends on how its tension compares with the load. Tension above the load shortens the muscle (concentric), tension equal to the load holds it (isometric), and tension below the load lets the load stretch the active muscle (eccentric). In every case the muscle must first build tension isometrically, and the heavier the load, the longer that takes and the slower the shortening that follows.
whyNot: Belongs. Isometric contractions still use ATP and generate force; the sarcomeres shorten a little while the elastic elements stretch, but the whole muscle length does not change.
Belongs. Concentric contraction is the shortening contraction, as in the lifting phase of a biceps curl.
Belongs. Lengthening under load is eccentric, as when you lower yourself down a stair.
Wrong. Velocity falls as load rises. This is the force velocity relationship: at maximal load velocity is zero and the contraction becomes isometric.
Belongs. The muscle cannot lift a load until its tension reaches the weight of that load, so there is always an isometric delay before shortening.
Wrong. Lowering a weight slowly is eccentric; the muscle is active but being lengthened. Concentric would be raising it.

stem: Which statements correctly compare skeletal muscle fiber types? Select all that apply.
options: Slow oxidative fibers have many mitochondria, dense capillaries, and abundant myoglobin, so they resist fatigue.
Fast glycolytic fibers have the largest diameter and produce the most force per fiber, but they fatigue quickly.
Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers combine a fast myosin ATPase with substantial mitochondrial content.
Slow oxidative fibers are recruited last because they belong to the largest motor units.
Fast glycolytic fibers depend mainly on oxidative phosphorylation for ATP.
Postural muscles that must hold tension for hours are dominated by slow oxidative fibers.
why: Fiber types differ in two independent properties: the speed of the myosin ATPase and the route used to make ATP. Slow oxidative fibers are slow, small, and built for aerobic endurance. Fast glycolytic fibers are fast, large, and built for brief maximal effort on glycolysis. Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers sit in between, fast but with enough mitochondria to last several minutes. A muscle's task predicts its fiber mix.
whyNot: Belongs. Every feature of a slow oxidative fiber supports steady aerobic ATP production, which is why these fibers can work for hours.
Belongs. Large diameter means more myofibrils in parallel and more force, but few mitochondria and few capillaries mean the fiber runs out of fuel and accumulates products fast.
Belongs. These fibers have fast myosin and a decent mitochondrial supply, so they fatigue more slowly than fast glycolytic fibers but faster than slow oxidative ones.
Wrong. Slow oxidative fibers are in the smallest motor units and are recruited first, which is why light sustained tasks use them almost exclusively.
Wrong. Fast glycolytic fibers have few mitochondria and rely on anaerobic glycolysis, which is why they fatigue in under a minute.
Belongs. Muscles such as the soleus and the deep back muscles need fatigue resistance far more than speed, so slow oxidative fibers dominate.

stem: Which statements about the ATP sources used by working muscle are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Creatine phosphate transfers its phosphate to ADP in a single enzyme step, so it is the fastest way to regenerate ATP.
Creatine phosphate stores are large enough to power about ten minutes of maximal effort.
Anaerobic glycolysis makes ATP faster than oxidative phosphorylation, but it yields only 2 ATP per glucose and produces lactate.
Oxidative phosphorylation is the slowest pathway to reach full rate but can sustain ATP supply for hours.
Oxidative phosphorylation needs oxygen delivered by the blood and can use fatty acids as well as glucose.
Resting muscle stores enough ATP to power several minutes of intense contraction.
why: Muscle keeps only a few seconds of ATP on hand, so it must regenerate ATP as fast as it uses it. Creatine phosphate is fastest but lasts about 10 to 15 seconds. Anaerobic glycolysis takes over within seconds and can carry a hard effort for a minute or two at the cost of lactate and falling pH. Oxidative phosphorylation is slow to ramp up and needs oxygen, but its yield per glucose is huge and it can also burn fat, so it sustains prolonged work.
whyNot: Belongs. Creatine kinase moves the phosphate straight onto ADP, with no pathway to run and no oxygen required.
Wrong. Creatine phosphate is exhausted in roughly 10 to 15 seconds of maximal work. Ten minutes is the domain of oxidative phosphorylation.
Belongs. Glycolysis is quick and oxygen independent but inefficient, and the pyruvate it makes is converted to lactate when it outruns the mitochondria.
Belongs. The mitochondria need the circulation to deliver oxygen and fuel, which takes a minute or more to ramp up, but the supply is then nearly unlimited.
Belongs. Aerobic muscle burns a mix of fatty acids and glucose, with fat making up a larger share as intensity falls.
Wrong. Stored ATP is used up within a few seconds. This option confuses the ATP store with the pathways that refill it.

stem: Which statements about smooth muscle types and their regulation are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Single unit smooth muscle cells are coupled by gap junctions, so a sheet of cells depolarizes and contracts together.
In multi unit smooth muscle each cell is stimulated separately by its own nerve supply, allowing fine, graded control.
Stretch can depolarize single unit smooth muscle and trigger contraction without any nerve input.
Hormones and local chemical signals can contract or relax smooth muscle without an action potential ever occurring.
Smooth muscle can only contract if it fires an action potential.
Multi unit smooth muscle shows spontaneous slow wave activity that spreads through the tissue.
why: Smooth muscle tone is set by many inputs at once. Single unit smooth muscle in the gut wall and small vessels is electrically coupled, often spontaneously active, and responds to stretch. Multi unit smooth muscle in the iris and airways is controlled cell by cell by nerves. In both, cytosolic Ca2+ can rise or fall through graded membrane potential changes or through receptor signaling, so contraction does not require an action potential.
whyNot: Belongs. Gap junctions let current pass cell to cell, so the sheet behaves as one unit.
Belongs. Independent innervation is what makes multi unit smooth muscle finely graded and what keeps it from contracting as a wave.
Belongs. Stretch opens mechanically gated channels and depolarizes the cell; this myogenic response helps arterioles regulate their own blood flow.
Belongs. Receptor coupled signals can open Ca2+ channels or release Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum directly, called pharmacomechanical coupling.
Wrong. Smooth muscle contraction is graded with cytosolic Ca2+, and Ca2+ can rise through slow depolarization or receptor signaling alone. Action potentials are one route, not the only one.
Wrong. Slow waves and pacemaker activity belong to single unit smooth muscle. Multi unit tissue waits for its nerves.

stem: Which statements correctly describe the levels of motor control? Select all that apply.
options: Spinal cord circuits can produce reflexes and rhythmic patterns such as stepping without input from the brain.
Brainstem nuclei adjust posture and balance and set background muscle tone during a movement.
The motor cortex plans and initiates voluntary movement and sends commands down descending tracts.
The cerebellum sends its output directly to spinal motor neurons to drive movement.
Higher levels of the hierarchy replace the spinal circuits rather than acting through them.
The decision to move begins in prefrontal and association cortex before the primary motor cortex is activated.
why: Movement is organized as a hierarchy. Association cortex decides, motor cortex commands, brainstem centers supply posture and tone, and spinal circuits carry out reflexes and rhythms. Every level ultimately works through the same spinal motor neurons, the final common pathway. The cerebellum and basal ganglia sit beside this chain and adjust it rather than driving motor neurons themselves.
whyNot: Belongs. Central pattern generators in the cord produce alternating flexor and extensor activity, and reflexes never leave the cord.
Belongs. Vestibular and reticular pathways from the brainstem hold you up so the cortex can concentrate on the skilled part of the movement.
Belongs. Primary motor cortex is the origin of the corticospinal tract that executes voluntary commands.
Wrong. The cerebellum has no direct route to spinal motor neurons. It corrects movements by acting on motor cortex and brainstem centers.
Wrong. Higher levels use the spinal circuits. A cortical lesion leaves the reflexes present and even exaggerated, which proves the spinal machinery was never bypassed.
Belongs. Planning areas are active before the primary motor cortex fires, which is why a decision to move can be detected before the movement begins.

stem: Which statements about the corticospinal pathway are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Corticospinal axons begin in the primary motor cortex and descend through the internal capsule and brainstem.
Most corticospinal fibers cross the midline at the pyramidal decussation in the medulla.
After crossing, the fibers travel in the lateral corticospinal tract and synapse on motor neurons or interneurons in the ventral horn.
The corticospinal tract crosses the midline at the level of the thalamus.
Because of the crossing, the left motor cortex controls muscles on the right side of the body.
Corticospinal axons synapse directly on the skeletal muscle fibers.
why: The corticospinal tract is a two neuron chain. The upper motor neuron runs from cortex through the internal capsule, cerebral peduncle, and pons to the medullary pyramids, where about 90 percent of the fibers cross. It then descends in the lateral corticospinal tract and synapses in the ventral horn on the lower motor neuron, which alone reaches the muscle. The crossing is why a stroke on one side weakens the opposite side of the body.
whyNot: Belongs. This is the route of the upper motor neuron from cortex to brainstem.
Belongs. The decussation at the bottom of the medulla is where left becomes right.
Belongs. The lateral tract carries the crossed fibers to the segment where the lower motor neuron lives.
Wrong. Crossing happens in the medulla, not the thalamus. The thalamus is a sensory relay and a target for basal ganglia and cerebellar output, not a corticospinal crossing point.
Belongs. Contralateral control follows directly from the decussation.
Wrong. Only the lower motor neuron contacts muscle. The corticospinal axon ends in the spinal cord, which is why upper and lower motor neuron lesions look different.

stem: Which statements about summation and tetanus in a skeletal muscle fiber are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Wave summation occurs when a second stimulus arrives before the fiber has fully relaxed from the first.
Summation happens because the Ca2+ released by the second action potential adds to Ca2+ still in the cytosol from the first.
Unfused tetanus shows a rippled tension record because the fiber partly relaxes between stimuli.
Fused tetanus requires the action potentials themselves to summate into one large depolarization.
Fused tetanic tension is several times the tension of a single twitch.
Raising the stimulus frequency beyond the fusion frequency keeps increasing tension without limit.
why: Because the action potential is over in a couple of milliseconds while the twitch lasts tens of milliseconds, a fiber can be re-excited while it is still contracting. Each new action potential releases more Ca2+ before SERCA has cleared the last batch, so Ca2+ builds up, more binding sites stay exposed, and tension climbs. At high enough frequency there is no relaxation at all and the record is a smooth plateau at maximal tension.
whyNot: Belongs. The overlap in time between one twitch and the next stimulus is the whole basis of summation.
Belongs. Cytosolic Ca2+ accumulates when release outruns reuptake, so more troponin is occupied.
Belongs. The ripples are partial relaxations, visible because the interval is a little longer than the time needed for Ca2+ to start falling.
Wrong. Action potentials are all or none and separated by refractory periods; they never summate. It is the mechanical response that summates.
Belongs. Sustained Ca2+ keeps almost every binding site open, and the elastic elements are fully stretched, so all the crossbridge force reaches the tendon.
Wrong. Once tension has fused at its maximum, every binding site that can be occupied already is, so more frequent stimuli add nothing. Beyond that point only fatigue can change the record.

stem: Which statements about the smooth muscle contraction mechanism are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Ca2+ binds calmodulin, and the Ca2+ calmodulin complex activates myosin light chain kinase.
Phosphorylation of the myosin light chain is required before smooth muscle myosin can cycle on actin.
Ca2+ for contraction enters from the extracellular fluid as well as being released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Ca2+ triggers smooth muscle contraction by binding to troponin on the thin filament.
Myosin light chain phosphatase promotes relaxation by removing the phosphate from myosin.
Smooth muscle myosin ATPase is faster than skeletal myosin ATPase, which is why smooth muscle contracts quickly.
why: Smooth muscle regulates contraction on the thick filament, not the thin filament. Ca2+ from outside the cell and from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds calmodulin, which switches on myosin light chain kinase. The kinase phosphorylates the myosin light chains, and only phosphorylated myosin can bind actin and cycle. A phosphatase reverses this. The enzyme cascade and the very slow myosin ATPase make the response slow but cheap.
whyNot: Belongs. Calmodulin is the Ca2+ sensor of smooth muscle, playing the role troponin plays in striated muscle.
Belongs. Unphosphorylated smooth muscle myosin sits folded and inactive; the phosphate is the on switch.
Belongs. Smooth muscle has a small sarcoplasmic reticulum and relies heavily on Ca2+ entry through membrane channels, which is why Ca2+ channel blockers relax blood vessels.
Wrong. Smooth muscle has no troponin. Ca2+ acts through calmodulin and the kinase instead.
Belongs. The balance between kinase and phosphatase sets how much myosin is active; slowing the phosphatase raises tension even at constant Ca2+.
Wrong. Smooth muscle myosin hydrolyzes ATP 10 to 100 times more slowly than skeletal myosin. That is why smooth muscle contracts slowly and why it can hold tension with so little ATP.

stem: Which statements about cardiac muscle are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Gap junctions in the intercalated discs let current pass from cell to cell, so one action potential spreads through the whole myocardium.
Desmosomes in the intercalated discs hold neighboring cells together so they do not pull apart during contraction.
The cardiac action potential lasts nearly as long as the contraction, so the refractory period prevents summation.
Cardiac muscle can be driven into fused tetanus by high frequency stimulation.
Cardiac contraction depends on Ca2+ entering from the extracellular fluid, which triggers further Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Each cardiac cell is separately innervated and contracts on its own schedule.
why: The heart works as a functional syncytium: a few pacemaker cells fire, and the impulse passes through gap junctions to every other cell, so the chamber contracts as one unit. The action potential has a long plateau carried by Ca2+ entry, and that Ca2+ entry triggers Ca2+ induced Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Because the cell stays refractory until the contraction is almost over, the heart can never tetanize, which is essential, since it must relax to fill.
whyNot: Belongs. Electrical coupling through gap junctions is what makes a single stimulus produce a coordinated beat.
Belongs. Desmosomes provide the mechanical link; gap junctions provide the electrical one.
Belongs. A 250 ms action potential covers most of a 300 ms contraction, so a second action potential cannot start until the first contraction is nearly finished.
Wrong. Tetanus needs a second action potential before relaxation, and the long refractory period makes that impossible. A tetanized heart could not pump.
Belongs. Cardiac muscle cannot contract in a Ca2+ free bath, unlike skeletal muscle, because trigger Ca2+ must enter through L type channels.
Wrong. Autonomic nerves modulate rate and force, but they do not tell individual cells when to contract. The coupled cells follow the pacemaker together.

stem: Which statements about how skeletal muscle adapts to training and disuse are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Endurance training raises mitochondrial content and capillary density with little change in fiber size.
Resistance training increases fiber cross sectional area by adding myofibrils in parallel.
Disuse causes loss of contractile protein and shrinkage of fibers within weeks.
Resistance training converts most fast fibers into slow oxidative fibers.
Strength gains from resistance training come mainly from a large increase in the number of muscle fibers.
Endurance training improves fatigue resistance by increasing the muscle's oxidative capacity.
why: Muscle remodels to match its workload. Prolonged low force activity builds the oxidative machinery: more mitochondria, more capillaries, more myoglobin. High force activity builds contractile protein, so fibers get thicker and stronger. Take the load away and both trends reverse quickly. Fiber number stays roughly fixed in adult humans, and fiber type shifts are limited, mostly between the two fast subtypes.
whyNot: Belongs. The endurance signature is oxidative capacity, not size; a marathon runner's fibers are not large.
Belongs. More myofibrils in parallel means more crossbridges pulling at once, which is more force.
Belongs. Bed rest or a cast produces measurable atrophy in a few weeks because protein synthesis falls below breakdown.
Wrong. Fiber type is set largely by the motor neuron, and training does not turn fast fibers slow. Resistance training mostly enlarges fast fibers.
Wrong. Growth is hypertrophy of existing fibers, not hyperplasia. A stronger muscle has bigger fibers, not many more of them.
Belongs. More mitochondria and capillaries let the fiber make ATP aerobically for longer before glycolytic products accumulate.

statement: The end plate potential is produced by acetylcholine opening voltage gated Na+ channels on the motor end plate.
correction: The end plate potential is produced by acetylcholine opening ligand gated nicotinic receptor channels; the voltage gated Na+ channels sit in the sarcolemma around the end plate and generate the muscle action potential.
why: Two different channels do two different jobs. The nicotinic receptor is opened by the chemical, not by voltage, and it produces a graded depolarization. That depolarization then spreads to the surrounding membrane and opens voltage gated Na+ channels, which fire the all or none action potential. Mixing these up hides why the end plate potential is graded and why a receptor blocker such as curare stops transmission without touching the Na+ channels.

statement: The latent period of a twitch is the delay between the stimulus and the start of tension, during which the action potential spreads and Ca2+ is released.
correction: True, because force cannot appear until the action potential has traveled down the T tubules, Ca2+ has been released, and the first crossbridges have attached.
why: The latent period is not dead time. The action potential is propagating along the sarcolemma and into the T tubules, the ryanodine receptors are opening, Ca2+ is binding troponin, and heads are beginning to attach. Only after all of that does tension at the tendon begin to rise. That is why the latent period is nearly fixed and does not depend on load or on how fast the myosin heads cycle.

statement: As the load on a muscle increases, the muscle shortens faster because more crossbridges are recruited to move it.
correction: As the load increases, the muscle shortens more slowly, and at a load equal to its maximal tension it does not shorten at all.
why: This is the force velocity relationship. A heavier load takes longer to lift because tension must first rise isometrically to match it, and the heads then cycle against more resistance, so shortening velocity falls as load rises. Recruiting more motor units raises the force available but does not reverse the relationship for a given muscle. At maximal load velocity is zero and the contraction is isometric.

statement: Fast glycolytic fibers are the most fatigue resistant fiber type because they contain the most mitochondria.
correction: Slow oxidative fibers are the most fatigue resistant because they have the most mitochondria; fast glycolytic fibers have few mitochondria and fatigue the fastest.
why: Fatigue resistance tracks oxidative capacity. Fast glycolytic fibers are built for brief powerful effort, so they carry a fast myosin, a large diameter, and little oxidative machinery, and they run down within a minute. Slow oxidative fibers trade speed and force for a dense supply of mitochondria, capillaries, and myoglobin, which is why they can hold posture all day.

statement: During the first few seconds of a sprint, creatine phosphate is the main source of new ATP because oxidative phosphorylation cannot increase its output quickly enough.
correction: True, because creatine kinase transfers a phosphate to ADP in one fast step, while oxidative phosphorylation needs a minute or more of increased blood flow and oxygen delivery to reach full rate.
why: Stored ATP lasts only a few seconds, so muscle needs an immediate backup. Creatine phosphate provides it: one enzyme, no oxygen, and a rate that matches even maximal ATP use. It runs out in 10 to 15 seconds, by which time anaerobic glycolysis has taken over, and oxidative phosphorylation gradually becomes dominant as the circulation and mitochondria catch up. This is why a 100 meter sprint barely uses oxygen while running.

statement: Single unit smooth muscle cells cannot contract unless each cell receives its own input from an autonomic neuron.
correction: Single unit smooth muscle cells are coupled by gap junctions and can be excited by neighboring cells, by stretch, or by pacemaker activity, so most cells contract without any direct nerve contact.
why: The statement describes multi unit smooth muscle, where each cell is independently innervated. Single unit smooth muscle in the gut, uterus, and small blood vessels behaves as an electrical sheet. Depolarization started by a pacemaker cell, a stretch, or a neurotransmitter released near a few cells spreads through gap junctions to the whole tissue. Nerves and hormones adjust this activity but are not required to start it.

statement: The spinal cord only relays commands from the brain to muscle and cannot generate a movement pattern on its own.
correction: Spinal cord circuits produce reflexes and rhythmic patterns such as stepping on their own; the brain starts, stops, and adjusts these patterns rather than building every movement from scratch.
why: The lowest level of the motor hierarchy does real work. Stretch and withdrawal reflexes are complete within the cord, and central pattern generators can produce alternating flexion and extension of the legs after the cord has been disconnected from the brain. Descending pathways from cortex and brainstem select which spinal circuits run and how strongly. That division of labor is why a cortical lesion leaves reflexes present, and even exaggerated.

statement: Most corticospinal axons cross the midline in the medulla, so the right motor cortex controls muscles on the left side of the body.
correction: True, because about 90 percent of the fibers cross at the pyramidal decussation before descending in the lateral corticospinal tract.
why: The upper motor neuron starts in the cortex on one side and ends on lower motor neurons on the opposite side of the cord. The crossing happens in the medulla, so a lesion above the decussation weakens the opposite side of the body while a lesion below it, in the cord, weakens the same side. Knowing where the tract crosses is what lets you locate a lesion from the pattern of weakness.

statement: A sarcomere generates its greatest active tension when it is stretched as far as possible, because titin is then fully extended and pulls hardest.
correction: A sarcomere generates its greatest active tension at an intermediate resting length where thick and thin filament overlap is optimal; at long lengths overlap is lost and active tension falls, while the rising tension from titin is passive, not active.
why: Active tension comes from crossbridges, and the number that can form depends on how much thin filament lies beside the thick filament. Stretch the sarcomere past optimal length and thin filaments pull away from the myosin heads, so active force drops toward zero. The tension you feel in an overstretched muscle is passive tension from titin and connective tissue, which is real force but not contraction. Separating the two curves is the whole point of the length tension relationship.

statement: Ca2+ triggers skeletal muscle contraction by binding directly to the myosin heads and switching on their ATPase.
correction: Ca2+ binds troponin on the thin filament, which shifts tropomyosin off the myosin binding sites on actin; the myosin heads are already energized and simply gain access to actin.
why: In skeletal muscle the switch is on the thin filament, not the thick one. Myosin heads hydrolyze ATP and sit cocked whether or not Ca2+ is present; what stops them at rest is tropomyosin covering their binding sites. Ca2+ binding to troponin moves tropomyosin aside and lets the cycle run. The statement describes something closer to smooth muscle, where Ca2+ acts on the myosin side through calmodulin and a kinase, and even there Ca2+ does not bind myosin itself.

prompt: Without notes, explain what a voltage series on a simulated whole muscle shows. Say why force is zero at low voltage, why it rises with voltage, and why it stops rising. Define threshold and maximal stimulus as you go.
rubric: below threshold no fiber reaches its firing threshold, so force is zero
threshold is the lowest voltage that produces any measurable force
each fiber is all or none, so rising voltage raises force by exciting more fibers (recruitment), not by making fibers contract harder
maximal stimulus is the lowest voltage at which every fiber is activated and force plateaus
voltages above maximal add no force because there are no fibers left to recruit
a whole muscle is graded by the number of active fibers even though each fiber is all or none

prompt: Without notes, trace smooth muscle contraction from a rise in cytosolic Ca2+ to crossbridge cycling, then explain why the process is slower and more economical than skeletal muscle contraction.
rubric: Ca2+ comes from extracellular fluid through membrane channels and from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Ca2+ binds calmodulin, not troponin
Ca2+ calmodulin activates myosin light chain kinase
the kinase phosphorylates myosin light chains, and only phosphorylated myosin can bind actin and cycle
slower because contraction waits on an enzyme cascade and smooth muscle myosin ATPase is very slow
economical because slow cycling and the latch state hold tension with little ATP use
relaxation requires Ca2+ removal and dephosphorylation by myosin light chain phosphatase

prompt: Without notes, compare skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle on four points: where the Ca2+ for contraction comes from, which protein Ca2+ binds, what controls contraction, and how fast contraction is.
rubric: Ca2+ source: skeletal from the sarcoplasmic reticulum only; cardiac from extracellular entry that triggers SR release; smooth from both extracellular fluid and SR
regulatory protein: skeletal and cardiac use troponin on the thin filament; smooth uses calmodulin and myosin light chain kinase

control: skeletal contracts only when a somatic motor neuron fires; cardiac is autorhythmic and modulated by autonomic nerves and hormones; smooth is controlled by autonomic nerves, hormones, local signals, and stretch
speed: skeletal fastest, cardiac intermediate, smooth slowest
skeletal muscle can be tetanized; cardiac cannot because of its long refractory period
cardiac and single unit smooth muscle are coupled by gap junctions; skeletal fibers are electrically isolated from each other

prompt: Without notes, contrast what the cerebellum and the basal ganglia contribute to movement. For each, describe one motor sign a lesion produces and explain why that sign follows from the structure's job.
rubric: cerebellum compares the intended movement with sensory feedback about the actual movement and corrects errors in timing and coordination
cerebellar lesion produces overshoot or undershoot, intention tremor, or clumsy rapid alternating movements, because errors are no longer corrected
cerebellar signs appear on the same side as the lesion
basal ganglia help select and initiate wanted movements and suppress unwanted ones, acting through the thalamus on the cortex
basal ganglia lesion produces slow, hard to start movement or unwanted involuntary movement, depending on which pathway is affected
neither structure drives spinal motor neurons directly, so strength and reflexes stay normal with either lesion

prompt: Without notes, walk through one turn of the crossbridge cycle. Say where ATP binds, where it is hydrolyzed, which step generates force, and what happens to the cycle when ATP runs out.
rubric: ATP binds the myosin head, and binding makes the head detach from actin
the head hydrolyzes ATP to ADP and Pi, which cocks the head into its high energy position
the cocked head binds actin when Ca2+ has exposed the binding site
release of Pi triggers the power stroke, which pulls the thin filament toward the center of the sarcomere
ADP is released and the head stays tightly bound until a new ATP arrives
without ATP the heads cannot detach, so the muscle locks in rigor
the cycle repeats as long as ATP is present and Ca2+ keeps the binding sites exposed

prompt: Without notes, explain how a skeletal muscle contraction ends. Include the roles of acetylcholinesterase and SERCA, and predict what happens to the muscle if each one stops working.
rubric: acetylcholinesterase breaks down acetylcholine in the cleft, so the end plate repolarizes and no new action potentials are triggered
SERCA pumps Ca2+ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum using ATP
as cytosolic Ca2+ falls, Ca2+ leaves troponin and tropomyosin covers the binding sites again
crossbridges stop forming and the fiber relaxes; relaxation therefore needs ATP
if acetylcholinesterase fails, the end plate stays depolarized, causing twitching and then weakness because Na+ channels stay inactivated
if SERCA fails, Ca2+ stays high in the cytosol, relaxation is slow, and repeated stimulation produces sustained contraction

prompt: Without notes, define a motor unit and explain how the nervous system grades the force of a whole muscle from a light touch to a maximal effort.
rubric: a motor unit is one motor neuron plus every muscle fiber it innervates
all fibers in a unit contract together, so the unit is the smallest amount of force the nervous system can add
small units (few fibers, slow oxidative) give fine control; large units (many fibers, fast) give big force
units are recruited in order of size, small first and large last (the size principle)
force is also graded by raising the firing rate of active units toward tetanus (rate coding)
asynchronous recruitment lets units take turns during sustained submaximal effort, which delays fatigue

prompt: Without notes, contrast an upper motor neuron lesion with a lower motor neuron lesion. Cover muscle tone, reflexes, muscle bulk, and any extra signs, and explain the mechanism behind each difference.
rubric: lower motor neuron lesion: flaccid, reduced tone, because the muscle has lost its only source of activation
lower motor neuron lesion: stretch reflex lost or reduced, because the efferent limb of the reflex arc is gone
lower motor neuron lesion: marked wasting and fasciculations, because the fiber loses the neuron's trophic support and denervated fibers fire spontaneously
upper motor neuron lesion: spasticity with increased tone, because descending inhibition of the spinal reflex circuits is lost
upper motor neuron lesion: brisk reflexes and an extensor plantar response, because the reflex arc is intact but released from descending control
upper motor neuron lesion: only mild disuse atrophy and no fasciculations, because the lower motor neuron still supplies the muscle

case: A 19 year old receiving a volatile anesthetic during a minor surgery develops rigid muscles all over. His core temperature climbs to 40.5 C (104.9 F) in 20 minutes, his end tidal CO2 doubles, and his serum creatine kinase later reads 8500 U/L (normal 30 to 200). He has a family history of the same reaction, traced to an abnormal ryanodine receptor that the anesthetic opens and holds open.
stem: Trace the mechanism from the abnormal channel to the rigidity and heat.
options: Ryanodine receptors stay open, so cytosolic Ca2+ stays high, crossbridges cycle continuously, and SERCA burns ATP trying to clear the Ca2+; the ATP turnover produces the heat.
The anesthetic blocks acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine builds up at the end plate and drives constant action potentials.
The DHP receptors fail to sense voltage, so no Ca2+ is released and the fibers lock in rigor from lack of ATP.
The T tubules collapse, so action potentials cannot reach the interior and the fibers contract only at their surface.
why: Everything follows from a release channel that will not close. The sarcoplasmic reticulum keeps leaking Ca2+ into the cytosol, troponin stays occupied, and crossbridges cycle without any action potentials, which is the rigidity. Two ATP consumers now run flat out: the myosin heads and SERCA, which pumps Ca2+ back only to have it leak out again. ATP hydrolysis on that scale releases heat and CO2, and the fibers eventually break down, which is why creatine kinase leaks into the blood.
whyNot: Correct. A leaky release channel bypasses the whole electrical side of coupling and produces contraction driven directly by Ca2+.

Wrong. That is the mechanism of organophosphate poisoning, and it acts at the junction, before the action potential. Here the defect is downstream, at the SR, and a neuromuscular blocker would not stop it.
Wrong. A failed voltage sensor gives paralysis, not rigidity, because Ca2+ is never released. Rigor from ATP loss is a late event, not the cause of the initial contraction.
Wrong. Broken T tubules would prevent contraction in the fiber's core; they would not produce sustained whole body rigidity or a runaway rise in metabolic rate.

case: About six hours after death, a body's skeletal muscles have become stiff and the joints resist being moved. Muscle ATP, measured in a sample, is below 5 percent of its living value, and cytosolic Ca2+ is high because the sarcoplasmic reticulum has leaked its store.
stem: Why are the muscles stiff, and which single change would allow the fibers to relax?
options: Without ATP the myosin heads cannot detach from actin, so nearly every head is locked in the bound state; supplying ATP would let the heads release.
Ca2+ is stuck on troponin, so the binding sites cannot be covered; removing Ca2+ alone would relax the fibers even without ATP.
The heads are frozen in the cocked, unbound state because there is no ATP to hydrolyze; adding Ca2+ would restart the cycle.
Acetylcholinesterase has stopped working, so the fibers are being continuously stimulated; blocking the receptors would relax them.
why: Detachment is the step that costs ATP. With Ca2+ high and binding sites open, every head that attaches completes its power stroke and then waits for an ATP that never arrives, so the fibers fill with bound heads and become rigid. This is rigor. Only ATP can break the bond; removing Ca2+ would stop new attachments but would not release the heads already bound. In life, rigor is what a muscle would do if it ever ran completely out of ATP, which is why cells guard their ATP so carefully.
whyNot: Correct. The bound, ADP free state is where the cycle stalls without ATP, and it is a rigid state because the heads are attached.
Wrong. Ca2+ controls whether heads can attach, not whether they can let go. Chelating Ca2+ in an ATP free fiber leaves the existing crossbridges locked in place.
Wrong. A head without ATP is bound to actin, not cocked and free. The cocked state is the product of ATP hydrolysis, which cannot happen here.
Wrong. There are no action potentials after death, and the junction is irrelevant. The stiffness comes from inside the fiber, at the crossbridges.

case: A 42 year old has a plasma Ca2+ of 1.6 mmol/L (normal 2.2 to 2.6) after thyroid surgery. She has tingling around her mouth and painful cramping spasms of her hands and feet. A classmate reasons that low Ca2+ should mean less Ca2+ for troponin, so her muscles ought to be weak, not spasming.
stem: Why does low plasma Ca2+ produce spasms rather than weakness?
options: The Ca2+ that binds troponin comes from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, not the plasma, so contraction is intact; low extracellular Ca2+ instead makes motor neurons and muscle membranes fire more easily, so the muscles are stimulated spontaneously.
Low plasma Ca2+ forces the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release all of its Ca2+ at once, producing a sustained contracture.
Low Ca2+ prevents tropomyosin from covering the binding sites, so crossbridges cycle without any stimulus.
Low Ca2+ blocks acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine accumulates and the end plates stay depolarized.
why: The two pools of Ca2+ have to be kept apart. Contraction uses Ca2+ stored inside the fiber in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and that store is not depleted by a low plasma level. Extracellular Ca2+ has a separate job: it stabilizes voltage gated Na+ channels. When it falls, the channels open with less depolarization, so nerves and muscle fibers fire spontaneously. The spasms are therefore a sign of hyperexcitable membranes driving a normal contractile system, and the fix is to raise plasma Ca2+, not to alter troponin.
whyNot: Correct. The contractile machinery is normal and the trouble is upstream, in the excitability of the membranes.
Wrong. The SR does not dump its store in response to low extracellular Ca2+; skeletal muscle release requires the voltage sensor signal, not extracellular Ca2+.
Wrong. Low cytosolic Ca2+ leaves tropomyosin in the blocking position. If anything, less Ca2+ means fewer exposed sites, so this would predict weakness, the opposite of what she has.

Wrong. Acetylcholinesterase is not Ca2+ dependent in this way. Enzyme failure would give a depolarizing block with weakness, and it would not explain the tingling, which is a sensory nerve sign of hyperexcitability.

case: An isolated skeletal fiber produces a twitch with a peak of 100 mN, reaching peak in 30 ms and returning halfway to baseline 25 ms later. The bath is then switched to one containing thapsigargin, a drug that blocks SERCA but does not affect the ryanodine receptor, the action potential, or the crossbridges. The fiber is stimulated again, once, and then five times at one second intervals.
stem: Predict the fiber's response after the drug.
options: The first twitch rises normally but relaxes very slowly, and the repeated stimuli produce a sustained contracture, because released Ca2+ cannot be returned to the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
The twitch is abolished, because the sarcoplasmic reticulum cannot release Ca2+ without SERCA.
The latent period becomes much longer, because Ca2+ must now diffuse across the whole fiber before binding troponin.
The fiber relaxes faster than before, because Ca2+ now leaves through the sarcolemma instead of waiting for the pump.
why: SERCA does one job: it ends the contraction by clearing Ca2+ from the cytosol. Release through the ryanodine receptor is untouched, so the first twitch starts on time and reaches a normal peak. But with the pump blocked Ca2+ stays on troponin, and relaxation is left to slow leakage out of the cell. Each further stimulus adds more Ca2+ to a cytosol that is not being cleared, so the fiber ratchets into a maintained contraction even at one stimulus per second, a frequency that never causes summation in a healthy fiber.
whyNot: Correct. Release is normal and removal is blocked, which separates the two halves of the Ca2+ cycle cleanly.

Wrong. Release depends on the store already loaded in the SR and on the ryanodine receptor opening. The pump refills the store afterward; it is not needed for the first release, and the store would run down only over many contractions.
Wrong. The latent period is set by the action potential and the release step, both normal here. Ca2+ still enters the cytosol right next to the myofibrils.
Wrong. The sarcolemmal Ca2+ pumps and exchangers are far too slow to replace SERCA, which is why relaxation becomes slower, not faster.

case: A fast twitch fiber has a twitch lasting 60 ms and fuses into a smooth tetanus at about 80 Hz. A drug that halves the rate of SERCA is applied. The single twitch now reaches the same peak tension, but its total duration doubles to 120 ms.
stem: Predict how the drug changes the stimulus frequency needed for fused tetanus, and why.
options: Fusion now occurs at a lower frequency, because each twitch lasts longer, so stimuli do not need to arrive as close together to catch the fiber before it relaxes.
Fusion now requires a higher frequency, because the slower pump means more Ca2+ must be released to reach the same tension.
The fusion frequency is unchanged, because it is set by the refractory period of the action potential, not by the twitch.
The fiber can no longer be tetanized, because slower Ca2+ removal reduces the amount of Ca2+ available for release.
why: Fusion happens when the next stimulus arrives before relaxation is complete. What sets that interval is the twitch duration, which depends mostly on how fast Ca2+ is pumped away. Halve the pump rate and the twitch lasts twice as long, so a stimulus arriving at half the old frequency still lands inside the previous twitch. The fiber therefore summates and fuses at a lower frequency. This is also why slow oxidative fibers, which have slower Ca2+ removal, fuse at lower frequencies than fast fibers.
whyNot: Correct. A longer twitch widens the window during which the next stimulus can summate.
Wrong. Peak tension was unchanged, so release is normal. Fusion is about timing, not about the amount released, and a slower pump makes Ca2+ accumulate more easily, not less.
Wrong. The refractory period lasts a few milliseconds and would allow hundreds of stimuli per second; it is never the limit. The twitch duration is.
Wrong. Over a short tetanus the SR store is not the limiting factor, and the drug slows refilling rather than abolishing it. The fiber tetanizes more easily, not less.

case: A 60 year old who had polio as a child lost about 70 percent of the motor neurons to her right thigh muscles. The surviving motor neurons sprouted branches and reinnervated many of the orphaned fibers, so a typical unit that once contained 500 fibers now contains 1200. Her maximal knee extension force is 80 percent of the left side.
stem: Predict how the reinnervation affects her ability to grade force at low levels, and why.
options: Grading becomes coarser, because each surviving unit now controls more fibers, so each recruitment step adds a larger jump in force.
Grading becomes finer, because there are fewer units and the nervous system can coordinate them more precisely.
Grading is unchanged, because reinnervated fibers restore the original number of units.
Grading is unchanged, because rate coding can fully replace recruitment at every force level.
why: The nervous system grades force mostly by choosing how many units to turn on, and the smallest increment it can add is one unit. Reinnervation rescued much of her maximal force by putting the orphaned fibers back under command, but it did so by making each unit much bigger. The first unit recruited now adds more than twice the force it once did, so low force tasks are harder to fine tune. Rate coding helps but cannot produce a step smaller than the smallest unit's twitch.
whyNot: Correct. Force resolution is set by unit size, and every unit got bigger.
Wrong. Fewer, larger units give coarser control, not finer. Precision comes from having many small units to choose from.
Wrong. Sprouting adds fibers to existing units; it does not create new motor neurons, so the number of units stays reduced.
Wrong. Rate coding adjusts the force of units already active, but the first step of any contraction is still the twitch of the smallest available unit, which is now large.

case: A student squeezes a grip dynamometer with the wrist in a neutral position and records 180 N. She repeats the test with the wrist fully flexed, which shortens the finger flexor muscles in the forearm, and records only 95 N. Her effort and motor unit activation, checked by EMG, are the same in both trials.
stem: Explain the drop in force in the flexed position.
options: At the shorter length thin filaments overlap each other and thick filaments run into the Z discs, so fewer effective crossbridges form and active tension falls.
Fewer motor units can be recruited when a muscle is shortened, so less of the muscle is active.
Passive tension from titin opposes the contraction at short length, subtracting from the measured force.
The sarcoplasmic reticulum releases less Ca2+ when the fiber is short, so fewer binding sites open.
why: Force at a given activation depends on sarcomere length. In the neutral position the flexors sit near optimal length, where every myosin head faces a thin filament. Flexing the wrist shortens them onto the ascending limb of the length tension curve: thin filaments from opposite sides begin to overlap and interfere with each other, and the thick filaments press against the Z discs, so crossbridges pull less effectively. EMG confirms the nervous system did its part; the deficit is mechanical, in the sarcomere.
whyNot: Correct. This is the ascending limb of the length tension curve, where geometry inside the sarcomere limits force.
Wrong. Recruitment is a nervous system decision and does not depend on muscle length, and the matched EMG shows activation was the same.
Wrong. Passive tension from titin appears when the muscle is stretched, not shortened. At short lengths passive tension is close to zero.
Wrong. Ca2+ release per action potential is set by the T tubule signal and does not change with sarcomere length in this range.

case: A volunteer holds a maximal handgrip for two minutes. Force falls from 450 N to 270 N. Throughout the test a brief electrical stimulus to the nerve is superimposed on her effort. At the start the stimulus adds 20 N to her voluntary force (about 4 percent); at the end it adds 25 N (about 9 percent of her remaining force). She reports that her hand simply stopped responding.
stem: Where is most of the fatigue located, and what does that say about its mechanism?
options: Mostly in the muscle fibers themselves, because the stimulated muscle could add only 25 N; the loss reflects changes inside the fiber such as phosphate accumulation and reduced Ca2+ release, not a failure of the nervous system to drive it.
Mostly central, because her report of the hand not responding shows the motor cortex stopped sending commands.
Mostly at the neuromuscular junction, because the extra force from nerve stimulation proves acetylcholine release was failing.
Entirely central, because the superimposed stimulus recovered more force at the end than at the start.
why: The superimposed stimulus asks one question: is there force the muscle can make that the nervous system is not asking for? Here the answer is a little, and it is a similar small amount at both ends of the test. So the muscle's own maximal output has fallen from about 470 N to about 295 N, and that loss is peripheral. Peripheral fatigue during a sustained maximal contraction comes from events inside the fiber: inorganic phosphate builds up and interferes with crossbridge force and with Ca2+ release, and the SR releases less Ca2+ per action potential. Her sensation of the hand not responding is real, but it reflects a muscle that cannot respond, not a brain that stopped asking.
whyNot: Correct. A small superimposed twitch throughout means the nervous system stayed close to maximal drive and the deficit is in the fiber.
Wrong. Central fatigue would show as a large superimposed twitch, meaning stimulation recovers a lot of force. A 25 N gain on a 180 N loss is small. Sensation is not a measurement of drive.
Wrong. Nerve stimulation works through the same junction; if the junction were failing the stimulus could not add force either. Junctional failure is not a normal feature of voluntary fatigue.
Wrong. The stimulus is a small fraction of force at both times. Calling it entirely central would require the stimulated muscle to still reach 450 N, and it reaches only about 295 N.

case: A 35 year old completes 12 weeks of cycling, 45 minutes a day at a moderate pace. Thigh biopsies before and after show mitochondrial volume density up 40 percent, capillaries per fiber up 25 percent, myoglobin up, fiber cross sectional area unchanged, and no change in the proportion of slow versus fast fibers.
stem: Predict the change in this person's muscle performance and explain it from the biopsy.
options: Much longer time to fatigue at a submaximal workload, with no change in maximal force, because the fibers can now make ATP aerobically for longer while their contractile protein content is unchanged.
Higher maximal force, because more mitochondria supply more ATP to the crossbridges.
Faster sprint speed, because the training added fast glycolytic fibers.
Shorter twitch duration, because the extra mitochondria speed up the myosin ATPase.
why: Read what changed and what did not. The oxidative machinery grew: more mitochondria to make ATP aerobically, more capillaries to deliver oxygen and fuel and clear products, more myoglobin to buffer oxygen inside the fiber. The contractile machinery did not grow, since fiber area is unchanged, and the fiber types did not shift. So the muscle can hold a moderate effort far longer before glycolytic products accumulate, but it cannot pull any harder than before. This is the endurance adaptation, and it is why endurance training and strength training are not interchangeable.
whyNot: Correct. Fatigue resistance rises with oxidative capacity; maximal force tracks contractile protein, which did not change.
Wrong. Maximal force is set by the number of crossbridges in parallel, which is fiber area. ATP supply is not the limit for a brief maximal effort.
Wrong. The biopsy shows no change in fiber type, and training does not create new fibers. Endurance work, if anything, pushes fast fibers toward the oxidative subtype.
Wrong. Twitch speed depends on the myosin isoform and on SERCA, neither of which mitochondria alter.

case: In lab, a student's maximal grip is 400 N. Asked to hold 50 percent (200 N), she keeps it steady for 55 seconds while her surface EMG amplitude climbs from 0.4 mV to 0.7 mV, then force falls below target. After a 10 minute rest she holds 20 percent (80 N). This time she lasts over 6 minutes, and EMG amplitude rises only slowly.
stem: Explain why the 20 percent hold lasts so much longer than the 50 percent hold.
options: At 20 percent the force is supplied by small, fatigue resistant oxidative units, and units can be rotated in and out, so the reserve of fresh units lasts far longer than at 50 percent, where large fast units must be recruited and fatigue quickly.
At 20 percent the EMG is lower, which means the muscle uses almost no ATP and cannot fatigue.
At 20 percent only fast glycolytic units are active, and they are the most fatigue resistant units.
The 10 minute rest trained the muscle, so it became stronger before the second trial.
why: Recruitment follows the size principle. A 20 percent target is met almost entirely by small slow oxidative units, which make ATP aerobically and can run for a long time, and because the pool is far from exhausted the nervous system can alternate units and let some rest. At 50 percent the fast, less oxidative units are already needed from the start; they fatigue within a minute, the rising EMG shows the system recruiting whatever reserve remains, and once that reserve is gone the target cannot be held. Time to failure therefore falls steeply as the target force rises.
whyNot: Correct. Both the type of units in use and the size of the unused reserve favor the low force hold.
Wrong. Lower EMG means fewer active units, not zero ATP use. The active units are working and would eventually fatigue; they just have a much larger safety margin.
Wrong. This reverses the size principle and the fiber properties. Fast glycolytic units are recruited last and fatigue fastest.
Wrong. Training adaptations take weeks. Ten minutes restores creatine phosphate and clears metabolites, but it does not make the muscle stronger than it was before the first trial.

case: An isolated strip of ventricular muscle has an action potential lasting 250 ms and a contraction lasting about 300 ms. A researcher stimulates it at 10 Hz, one stimulus every 100 ms, the same frequency that fuses a skeletal muscle strip from the same animal into a smooth tetanus.
stem: Predict the cardiac strip's tension record and explain the difference from skeletal muscle.
options: The strip responds only to stimuli that arrive after its refractory period ends, so it produces separate beats at a lower rate than 10 Hz and never fuses.
The strip produces a smooth fused tetanus, because Ca2+ accumulates in the cytosol just as it does in skeletal muscle.
The strip produces an unfused tetanus with a rippled record, because partial relaxation occurs between stimuli.
The strip stops contracting after the first beat, because its sarcoplasmic reticulum is emptied and cannot refill at this rate.
why: The skeletal action potential is over in 2 ms, so a stimulus every 100 ms finds the fiber excitable and still contracting, and the twitches summate. The cardiac cell is refractory for nearly the whole 250 ms plateau, so stimuli arriving at 100 ms intervals are simply ignored until the membrane has repolarized. By then the previous contraction is almost finished, so each accepted stimulus produces a fresh, separate beat. This long refractory period is what guarantees the heart relaxes and fills between beats.
whyNot: Correct. The refractory period, not the stimulus rate, decides when the cell can fire again, and it outlasts most of the contraction.
Wrong. Summation needs a second action potential during the contraction, and the refractory period forbids it. Cardiac cells cannot fuse at any frequency.
Wrong. Unfused tetanus still needs re-excitation before relaxation is complete, which the refractory period prevents. The record shows separated beats, not ripples on a raised baseline.
Wrong. Trigger Ca2+ enters from outside the cell each beat and the store refills between beats. The strip keeps beating; it just beats at the rate the refractory period allows.

case: A 55 year old is examined three months after a stroke. His right leg is weak. Tone in the leg is increased and catches when the examiner moves it quickly. The right knee reflex is graded 4+ (normal 2+), and stroking the sole of the right foot makes the big toe extend. Muscle bulk in the right leg is nearly the same as the left, and there are no fasciculations.
stem: Explain why the reflexes in the weak leg are exaggerated rather than lost.
options: The lesion is above the spinal cord, so the reflex arc and its lower motor neurons are intact but have lost descending inhibition, and the released spinal circuits overreact to stretch.
Motor neurons in the ventral horn are dying, and the surviving ones fire more easily, which makes the reflex brisk.
The muscle spindles have been damaged and are sending a constant stream of signals to the cord.
The corticospinal tract is intact, and the problem lies in the muscle, which has become stiff and overreactive.
why: The findings are a set that goes together. Weakness with preserved bulk and no fasciculations says the lower motor neurons still supply the muscle. Increased tone, a brisk reflex, and an extensor plantar response say the descending pathways that normally damp the spinal reflex circuits are gone. That combination places the lesion in the upper motor neuron, here the corticospinal system damaged by the stroke. The reflex arc survives and, freed from inhibition, produces more response to the same stretch than it should.
whyNot: Correct. Upper motor neuron signs are release signs: the spinal cord is doing more, not less, once the brain stops holding it back.
Wrong. Loss of ventral horn motor neurons would break the efferent limb of the reflex and produce a reduced or absent reflex, along with wasting and fasciculations, none of which he has.
Wrong. Damaged spindles would reduce the afferent signal and weaken the reflex. Spindles are normal here; the cord is simply responding to their input without restraint.
Wrong. A muscle disease would not produce an extensor plantar response or increased reflexes, and the weakness after a stroke is a nervous system problem.
